public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 391

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/391](https://www.erdosproblems.com/391)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Er96b] Erdős, Paul, *Some problems I presented or planned to present in my short talk*.
  Analytic number theory, Vol. 1 (Allerton Park, IL, 1995) (1996), 333-335.
- [AlGr77] Alladi, Krishnaswami and Grinstead, Charles, *On the decomposition of $n!$ into prime
  powers*. J. Number Theory (1977), 452-458.
- [ACRSTUV25] B. Alexeev, E. Conway, M. Rosenfeld, A. Sutherland, T. Tao, M. Uhr, and K.
  Ventullo, *Decomposing a factorial into large factors*. arXiv:2503.20170 (2025).
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter Topology

namespace Erdos391

/-- `t n` is the largest `t` such that `n!` is a product of `n` factors all at least `t`,
i.e. the maximal $a_1$ in a representation $n! = a_1 \cdots a_n$ with $a_1 \leq \cdots \leq a_n$. -/
noncomputable def t (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {k : ℕ | ∃ a : Fin n → ℕ, ∏ i, a i = n.factorial ∧ ∀ i, k ≤ a i}

/--
Let $t(n)$ be maximal such that there is a representation
$$n!=a_1\cdots a_n$$
with $t(n)=a_1\leq \cdots \leq a_n$. Obtain good bounds for $t(n)/n$. In particular, is it true
that
$$\lim \frac{t(n)}{n}=\frac{1}{e}?$$

It is easy to see that $\lim \frac{t(n)}{n}\leq \frac{1}{e}$. Erdős [Er96b] wrote he, Selfridge,
and Straus had proved a corresponding lower bound, so that $\lim \frac{t(n)}{n}=\frac{1}{e}$, and
'believed that Straus had written up our proof. Unfortunately Straus suddenly died and no trace
was ever found of his notes. Furthermore, we never could reconstruct our proof, so our assertion
now can be called only a conjecture.'

Alladi and Grinstead [AlGr77] have obtained similar results when the $a_i$ are restricted to
prime powers.

Both questions were answered by Alexeev, Conway, Rosenfeld, Sutherland, Tao, Uhr, and Ventullo
[ACRSTUV25], who proved that
$$\frac{t(n)}{n}= \frac{1}{e}-\frac{c_0}{\log n}+O\left(\frac{1}{(\log n)^{1+c}}\right),$$
where $c_0=0.3044\cdots$ is an explicit constant, for some $c>0$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos391.lean#L4924"]
theorem erdos_391 : answer(True) ↔
    Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (t n : ℝ) / n) atTop (𝓝 (1 / Real.exp 1)) := by
  sorry

/--
Furthermore, does there exist some constant $c>0$ such that
$$\frac{t(n)}{n} \leq \frac{1}{e}-\frac{c}{\log n}$$
for infinitely many $n$?

This was answered in the affirmative by Alexeev, Conway, Rosenfeld, Sutherland, Tao, Uhr, and
Ventullo [ACRSTUV25].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos391.lean#L4924"]
theorem erdos_391.variants.deficit : answer(True) ↔ ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧
    {n : ℕ | (t n : ℝ) / n ≤ 1 / Real.exp 1 - c / Real.log n}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos391

reformulations.difference: The source defines t(n) as the largest a₁ over sorted representations n! = a₁⋯aₙ with a₁ ≤ ⋯ ≤ aₙ. The Lean defines `t n` as the `sSup` of all k for which some unsorted tuple `a : Fin n → ℕ` with product n! has every entry ≥ k. At n = 0 the Lean set is all of ℕ (empty product 1 = 0!), so the `sSup` falls back to the junk value `t 0 = 0`; the source leaves t(0) undefined.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Take n ≥ 1. The set is nonempty (k = 0 via the tuple 1,2,…,n) and bounded by n!, since each aᵢ divides n! > 0. So the `sSup` is an attained maximum. A sorted representation has a₁ = min aᵢ, so a₁ lies in the Lean set. Conversely, sorting a witness (`Tuple.sort`) keeps the product, and its first entry is ≥ k. I proved in Lean that for n ≥ 1, `t n` is `IsGreatest` of {a ⟨0,_⟩ | a monotone, ∏ a = n!}, which is the source's t(n). I also checked t 1 = t 2 = t 3 = 1 and t 4 = 2, matching OEIS A034258 (1,1,1,2,…) as quoted in arXiv:2503.20170. The junk value at n = 0 cannot affect either theorem. A limit ignores one term. In the deficit variant, n = 0 is always in the set (0 ≤ 1/e − c/0 = 1/e) and n = 1 never is (1 > 1/e); neither changes whether the set is infinite.

review.notes:
No defects found. Both theorems match erdosproblems.com/391 word for word. The site asks two questions: "is it true that lim t(n)/n = 1/e?" and "does there exist some constant c>0 such that t(n)/n ≤ 1/e − c/log n for infinitely many n?". Its revision history shows this wording has not changed. The site marks the problem PROVED (LEAN), and ACRSTUV25 answered both questions affirmatively: t(N)/N = 1/e − c₀/log N + O(1/log^{1+c} N) with c₀ ≈ 0.304 > 0. So `answer(True)` is right in both theorems, and the `research solved` tags are current.

The linked formal proof (plby/lean-proofs, L4924) proves the conjunction of both statements. Its `t` agrees with this file's `t` for every n ≥ 1; the two differ only at n = 0 (1 there, 0 here), which changes neither statement. Precedence is as intended: `1 / Real.exp 1 - c / Real.log n` parses as (1/e) − (c/log n). Junk values affect only n = 0 and n = 1, so nothing is vacuous.

One point on the primary literature, for the record. I rendered ErGr80 p. 75 from the scan. It defines t(n) = max{a₁ : n! = ∏ aᵢ, a₁ ≤ ⋯ ≤ aₙ}, states the Erdős–Selfridge–Straus limit 1/e as an unpublished theorem, and then asks only "Can t(n) = n/e − cn/log n?". The relation is a plain "=", and no quantifier over n follows. erdosproblems.com reads this as "≤ … for infinitely many n"; the ACRSTUV25 paper reads it as "for some c>0 and sufficiently large N". The file follows erdosproblems.com, its main cited source, which is the repository convention. Every reading was settled affirmatively by the same paper, so the answer does not change. I report this as a note, not a finding. I could not access Er96b or Guy's B22 to see where the "infinitely many" wording comes from; this does not affect the verdict.
